We follow it from draft to merged or closed, and at each step ask the question of this whole part: is this GitHub data, or does it write to a branch?

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Assuming a required review covers the final diff. Root cause: an approval is attached to the diff as it was; without one of the two settings, a later push does not affect it.
Treating "changes requested" as a lock. Root cause: it is informational unless a rule requires a pull request.
Expecting green checks to carry over after a push. Root cause: checks are attached to a commit ID, and a push creates a new head commit.
Treating a null mergeable as "not mergeable" in a script. Root cause: null means the computation is still running.
Pushing after applying a suggestion or pressing Update branch, and being rejected. Root cause: GitHub made a commit on the branch; the local branch lacks it until you pull.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. The team from the hook enables "dismiss stale approvals" on main.
The textbook's advice is to name the cost when you propose the setting, and the team does: for small pull requests the re-review takes a minute and they keep it.
A second rule from the same section goes into their contribution guide: do not resolve conflicts in lock files or other generated files by picking a side.
Your turn. Do Exercise 21.2, "Is it still approved?", in exercises/m19-m25-github.md.
The challenge is Exercise 21.7, "Green on the pull request, red on main", in the same file.
Question 270 of the CTO question bank:

quotes: "A reviewer approved, the author pushed another commit, and the pull request merged. Which two settings address this, and what does each cost?"

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: Every state of a pull request is GitHub data; only the merge writes to a branch.
An approval belongs to a diff; "dismiss stale approvals" removes it when the diff changes, and "approval of the most recent reviewable push" requires someone other than the last pusher to approve.
Actions produces checks; both checks and statuses belong to commit IDs, and required checks must pass on the latest commit.
Mergeable means Git can merge the tips and the rules allow it.
A conflict is repaired on the head branch, by merging the base in or by rebasing; the reviewer sees the same diff either way.

beats.text: The lifecycle, in one sentence: a pull request moves from draft to ready for review, collects reviews and checks, and ends merged or closed.
beats.tele: The lifecycle, in one sentence: a pull request moves from draft to ready for review, collects reviews and checks, and ends merged or closed.

beats.text: Draft. "Draft pull requests cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically requested to review them." Code owners are the users or teams a repository assigns to paths. Marking the pull request ready "will request reviews from any code owners", and you can convert a pull request back to a draft at any time. Use a draft when you want CI and early comments but not a formal review. An outdated-advice note: since the first of May 2025, drafts are available in every repository, not only on paid plans.

Use a draft when you want CI and early comments but not a formal review. An outdated-advice note: since the first of May 2025, drafts are available in every repository, not only on paid plans.

beats.text: Reviews. A review has one of three outcomes. Comment: feedback without a verdict, which does not block. Approve: counts toward required approvals, if a rule requires any. Request changes: blocks only if a rule requires a pull request. GitHub's own words on that third outcome: it "is purely informational and will not prevent merging unless a ruleset or classic branch protection rule is configured with the 'require a pull request' option". Without a rule, "changes requested" is a request, not a lock.

Without a rule, "changes requested" is a request, not a lock.

beats.text: Two more documented facts: anyone with read access can review and comment, and "pull request authors cannot approve their own pull requests". That is why the review labs need a second account.

beats.text: Suggestions. A reviewer can propose replacement lines. When the author applies them, GitHub creates a single commit on the pull request's branch, on GitHub's side. Your local branch lacks it until you pull, and a push without pulling is rejected as a non-fast-forward.

beats.text: Stale approvals. In one sentence: an approval is attached to the diff, the set of changes, as it was when the reviewer approved. Two optional settings decide what happens to that approval when the diff changes afterwards.
beats.tele: Stale approvals. In one sentence: an approval is attached to the diff, the set of changes, as it was when the reviewer approved. Two optional settings decide what happens to that approval when the diff changes afterwards.

beats.text: Setting 1: dismiss stale approvals. GitHub records the state of the diff at the point of approval. If the diff changes from this state, the approving review is dismissed as stale, and the pull request cannot be merged until someone approves again. Listen to the causes the documentation gives: a contributor pushes new changes, someone clicks Update branch, or a related pull request is merged into the target branch. The diff can change without anyone touching your branch.
beats.tele: Setting 1: dismiss stale approvals. GitHub records the state of the diff at the point of approval. If the diff changes from this state, the approving review is dismissed as stale, and the pull request cannot be merged until someone approves again. Listen to the causes the documentation gives: a contributor pushes new changes, someone clicks Update branch, or a related pull request is merged into the target branch. The diff can change without anyone touching your branch.

beats.text: Setting 2: require approval of the most recent reviewable push. It requires "an approval from someone other than the last person to push to a branch". With this option stale reviews are not dismissed, and the pull request remains approved as long as someone other than the person who made the most recent changes approves it. GitHub presents it as a compromise for large pull requests with many reviewers, and says which one is stricter: "it is safer to dismiss stale reviews."
beats.tele: Setting 2: require approval of the most recent reviewable push. It requires "an approval from someone other than the last person to push to a branch". With this option stale reviews are not dismissed, and the pull request remains approved as long as someone other than the person who made the most recent changes approves it. GitHub presents it as a compromise for large pull requests with many reviewers, and says which one is stricter: "it is safer to dismiss stale reviews."

beats.text: The costs. The first costs a re-review after every update, including an "Update branch". The second can leave earlier approvals standing on a diff that has since changed.
beats.tele: The costs. The first costs a re-review after every update, including an "Update branch". The second can leave earlier approvals standing on a diff that has since changed.

beats.text: Quick quiz, back to the hook. Neither setting is on. A reviewer approves, then the author pushes again. Is the pull request still approved? A: yes. B: no. Your answer?

beats.text: A. The approval stands, on a diff that has since changed. That's how unread code reached main.
beats.tele: A. The approval stands, on a diff that has since changed. That's how unread code reached `main`.

beats.text: Checks and mergeability. In one sentence: mergeability is two independent questions. Can Git merge the two tips, which is the test merge? And do the repository's rules allow it?
beats.tele: Checks and mergeability. In one sentence: mergeability is two independent questions. Can Git merge the two tips, which is the test merge? And do the repository's rules allow it?

beats.text: GitHub distinguishes two kinds of status checks. Checks carry detailed output and are created by GitHub Apps, including Actions. Commit statuses are a simpler state set through the API by external services. "GitHub Actions generates checks, not commit statuses." Both are attached to a commit ID, not to the pull request. A new push creates a new head commit with no checks yet. And "required checks must pass on the latest commit SHA. Checks from earlier commits don't satisfy the requirement."

A new push creates a new head commit with no checks yet. And "required checks must pass on the latest commit SHA. Checks from earlier commits don't satisfy the requirement."

beats.text: A red check blocks nothing by itself. Only a rule that names the check does.
beats.tele: A red check blocks nothing by itself. Only a rule that names the check does.

beats.text: For scripts: the API's mergeable field can be true, false or null. Null means GitHub has started a background job to compute it. A script that treats null as "not mergeable" is wrong. It must ask again.

beats.text: One caveat the textbook marks unverified: two GitHub pages disagree about how long checks data is retained, 400 days on one, the Actions retention setting of 90 days by default on a changelog entry effective the first of October 2026. The practical consequence either way: an old pull request may need its checks re-run before it can merge.

beats.text: Conflicts. On screen is today's example: two commits on the branch fix/threshold, one new commit on main. In one sentence: a pull request "has conflicts" when the test merge of head into base cannot be computed cleanly, and you repair it by changing the head branch, either by merging the base into it or by rebasing it onto the base.

beats.text: It is the ordinary three-way conflict from the merge videos, detected on the server, where nobody can resolve it. The resolution has to arrive as new commits on the head branch. GitHub offers three routes. The web conflict editor, which merges the entire base branch into the head branch and handles only simple competing line changes. The command line. And, with the Copilot cloud agent, a button that has the agent commit a resolution, which you review like any resolution.

beats.text: That is the 🔴 command. The five answers. What it changes: it replaces the remote branch, if the remote branch is where you last saw it. What it can destroy: commits on the server that no clone of yours has. And alone, the check passes wrongly after a background fetch.

Rebase head onto base: the push is forced, commit IDs are replaced, the resolution is folded into the rewritten commits, and the commit list stays clean.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Assuming a required review covers the final diff. Root cause: an approval is attached to the diff as it was; without one of the two settings, a later push does not affect it.
beats.tele: Assuming a required review covers the final diff. Root cause: an approval is attached to the diff as it was; without one of the two settings, a later push does not affect it.

beats.text: Treating a null mergeable as "not mergeable" in a script. Root cause: null means the computation is still running.
